claim: The Atlantic herring is one of the most abundant vertebrates on earth.
source: The Atlantic herring is one of the most abundant vertebrates on earth but its nucleotide diversity is moderate (π = 0.3%), only three-fold higher than in human.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the Atlantic herring's abundance.

claim: The nucleotide diversity of Atlantic herring is moderate (π = 0.3%).
source: The Atlantic herring is one of the most abundant vertebrates on earth but its nucleotide diversity is moderate (π = 0.3%), only three-fold higher than in human.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016) mentioned later in the text.

claim: The nucleotide diversity of Atlantic herring is only three-fold higher than in human.
source: The Atlantic herring is one of the most abundant vertebrates on earth but its nucleotide diversity is moderate (π = 0.3%), only three-fold higher than in human.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on known data for both species.

claim: The estimated mutation rate in Atlantic herring is 2.0 × 10-9 per base per generation based on whole-genome sequencing of four parents and 12 offspring.
source: Based on whole-genome sequencing of four parents and 12 offspring, the estimated mutation rate is 2.0 × 10-9 per base per generation.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from pedigree sequencing.

claim: A high degree of parental mosaicism was observed in Atlantic herring, indicating that a large fraction of de novo mutations occurred during early germ cell development.
source: We observed a high degree of parental mosaicism indicating that a large fraction of these de novo mutations occurred during early germ cell development.
evidence: This is based on the observation that multiple offspring shared the same mutations at frequencies lower than expected for fixed mutations.

claim: The estimated mutation rate in Atlantic herring is the lowest among vertebrates analyzed to date.
source: The estimated mutation rate – the lowest among vertebrates analyzed to date – partially explains the discrepancy between the rather low nucleotide diversity in herring and its huge census population size.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with mutation rates from other vertebrate species presented in Table 3.

claim: The low mutation rate partially explains the discrepancy between the rather low nucleotide diversity in herring and its huge census population size.
source: The estimated mutation rate – the lowest among vertebrates analyzed to date – partially explains the discrepancy between the rather low nucleotide diversity in herring and its huge census population size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between mutation rate, population size, and nucleotide diversity.

claim: A species like the herring will never reach its expected nucleotide diversity because of fluctuations in population size over the millions of years it takes to build up high nucleotide diversity.
source: But a species like the herring will never reach its expected nucleotide diversity because of fluctuations in population size over the millions of years it takes to build up high nucleotide diversity.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference based on population genetics principles and the time required to reach equilibrium.

claim: The census population size of Atlantic herring is about 1012.
source: The Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus) is a good example of the paradox, since, in spite of an enormous census population size about 1012 (Supplementary file 1), its nucleotide diversity (π = 0.3%)(Martinez Barrio et al., 2016) is middle-of-the-road when compared to terrestrial mammals, e.g. 0.1% for humans (Hernandez et al., 2011) and 0.9% for European rabbits (Carneiro et al., 2014) with much smaller census populations.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The nucleotide diversity of Atlantic herring (π = 0.3%) is middle-of-the-road when compared to terrestrial mammals.
source: The Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus) is a good example of the paradox, since, in spite of an enormous census population size about 1012 (Supplementary file 1), its nucleotide diversity (π = 0.3%)(Martinez Barrio et al., 2016) is middle-of-the-road when compared to terrestrial mammals, e.g. 0.1% for humans (Hernandez et al., 2011) and 0.9% for European rabbits (Carneiro et al., 2014) with much smaller census populations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on nucleotide diversity in humans and European rabbits.

claim: Human nucleotide diversity is 0.1%.
source: The Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus) is a good example of the paradox, since, in spite of an enormous census population size about 1012 (Supplementary file 1), its nucleotide diversity (π = 0.3%)(Martinez Barrio et al., 2016) is middle-of-the-road when compared to terrestrial mammals, e.g. 0.1% for humans (Hernandez et al., 2011) and 0.9% for European rabbits (Carneiro et al., 2014) with much smaller census populations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hernandez et al., 2011.

claim: European rabbit nucleotide diversity is 0.9%.
source: The Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus) is a good example of the paradox, since, in spite of an enormous census population size about 1012 (Supplementary file 1), its nucleotide diversity (π = 0.3%)(Martinez Barrio et al., 2016) is middle-of-the-road when compared to terrestrial mammals, e.g. 0.1% for humans (Hernandez et al., 2011) and 0.9% for European rabbits (Carneiro et al., 2014) with much smaller census populations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carneiro et al., 2014.

claim: The extremely low genetic differentiation at selectively neutral loci between geographically distant populations strongly suggests that current Ne must be high and genetic drift very low in the Atlantic herring.
source: A large census population does not necessarily mean that the long term effective population size (Ne) is large but the extremely low genetic differentiation at selectively neutral loci between geographically distant populations strongly suggests that current Ne must be high and genetic drift very low in the Atlantic herring (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on data from Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: Before the NextGenerationSequencing-era, mutation rates were estimated by comparative genomics, by relating sequence differences to fossil record-dated estimates of species divergence times, or by tracking changes at specific loci in experimental studies.
source: Before the NextGenerationSequencing-era, mutation rates were estimated by comparative genomics, by relating sequence differences to fossil record-dated estimates of species divergence times, or by tracking changes at specific loci in experimental studies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about historical methods for estimating mutation rates.

claim: Historical methods for estimating mutation rates have limited accuracy because species divergence is hard to date and the use of a small subset of loci can introduce bias.
source: However, since species divergence is hard to date and the use of a small subset of loci can introduce bias, these methods have limited accuracy (Drake et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drake et al., 1998.

claim: Affordable whole genome sequencing has facilitated two approaches to estimate mutation rates: mutation accumulation lines and parent-offspring comparisons.
source: More recently, affordable whole genome sequencing has facilitated two approaches to estimate mutation rates: mutation accumulation lines and parent-offspring comparisons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about modern methods for estimating mutation rates.

claim: The mutation accumulation approach has the advantage of scalability, since it is possible to increase the number of mutation events observed by including more generations.
source: The mutation accumulation approach, where an inbred line is maintained for a number of generations and the mutation rate is measured by counting up differences between the first and last generation, has the advantage of scalability, since it is possible to increase the number of mutation events observed by including more generations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mutation accumulation method.

claim: The mutation accumulation approach requires an organism that can be reproduced as viable inbred lines.
source: On the other hand, the approach requires an organism that can be reproduced as viable inbred lines, and it is difficult to fully eliminate purifying selection against deleterious new mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of the mutation accumulation method.

claim: It is difficult to fully eliminate purifying selection against deleterious new mutations in the mutation accumulation approach.
source: On the other hand, the approach requires an organism that can be reproduced as viable inbred lines, and it is difficult to fully eliminate purifying selection against deleterious new mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of the mutation accumulation method.

claim: The parent-offspring approach has become the preferred method for estimating the mutation rate in non-model organisms.
source: The parent-offspring approach, which relies on using high coverage whole-genome sequencing to detect differences between parents and their offspring, alleviates the cultivation related issues, and has thus become the preferred method for estimating the mutation rate in non-model organisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about current practices in mutation rate estimation.

claim: The total number of mutation events per progeny will typically be small in the parent-offspring approach.
source: The trade-off is that the total number of mutation events per progeny will typically be small.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of the parent-offspring method.

claim: The available data on mutation rates is somewhat biased towards unicellular organisms, insects and mammals.
source: Currently, the number of studies using any of the methods outlined above remains small, and the available data is somewhat biased towards unicellular organisms (Dettman et al., 2016; Dillon et al., 2015; Farlow et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2012; Ness et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2014), insects (Keightley et al., 2014, 2015, 2009) and mammals (Harland et al., 2016; Kong et al., 2012; Uchimura et al., 2015; Venn et al., 2014), while including a single plant (Ossowski et al., 2010) and one bird (Smeds et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: This study is, to the authors' knowledge, the first of its kind in a teleost.
source: In this study, to our knowledge the first of its kind in a teleost, we estimate the genome-wide point mutation rate in Atlantic herring.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The Atlantic herring was chosen due to its suitability as a population genetic model system.
source: The Atlantic herring was chosen due to its suitability as a population genetic model system; it is one of the most abundant vertebrate species on earth with external reproduction involving large numbers of gametes per reproducing adult.
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing this species.

claim: The Atlantic herring has external reproduction involving large numbers of gametes per reproducing adult.
source: The Atlantic herring was chosen due to its suitability as a population genetic model system; it is one of the most abundant vertebrate species on earth with external reproduction involving large numbers of gametes per reproducing adult.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Atlantic herring reproduction.

claim: The Atlantic herring is one of the best approximations of a randomly mating, infinite size population among vertebrates.
source: In essence, these properties make the Atlantic herring one of the best approximations of a randomly mating, infinite size population among vertebrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the species' characteristics.

claim: There exists a high-quality draft genome assembly for Atlantic herring.
source: In addition, there exists a high-quality draft genome assembly (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016), which is a pre-requisite for a study of this kind.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: The spontaneous mutation rate in Atlantic herring is estimated to be 2.0 × 10−9 per site per generation.
source: We here estimate the spontaneous mutation rate to be 2.0 × 10−9 per site per generation in the Atlantic herring, six-fold lower than the rate in humans and the lowest rate reported so far for a vertebrate.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The mutation rate in Atlantic herring is six-fold lower than the rate in humans.
source: We here estimate the spontaneous mutation rate to be 2.0 × 10−9 per site per generation in the Atlantic herring, six-fold lower than the rate in humans and the lowest rate reported so far for a vertebrate.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the estimated mutation rate for herring and known human mutation rate.

claim: The mutation rate in Atlantic herring is the lowest rate reported so far for a vertebrate.
source: We here estimate the spontaneous mutation rate to be 2.0 × 10−9 per site per generation in the Atlantic herring, six-fold lower than the rate in humans and the lowest rate reported so far for a vertebrate.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with mutation rates from other vertebrate species.

claim: Two-generation experimental pedigrees were generated for spring-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring, each comprising the two parents and six offspring.
source: We have generated two-generation experimental pedigrees for spring-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring (classified as a subspecies of the Atlantic herring by Linnaeus (1761)), each comprising the two parents and six offspring (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Baltic herring is classified as a subspecies of the Atlantic herring by Linnaeus (1761).
source: We have generated two-generation experimental pedigrees for spring-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring (classified as a subspecies of the Atlantic herring by Linnaeus (1761)), each comprising the two parents and six offspring (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Linnaeus (1761).

claim: Each individual was sequenced to ~45–71 x coverage.
source: We performed whole-genome sequencing of these two pedigrees using genomic DNA isolated from muscle tissue. As detection of de novo mutations requires high sequence coverage, we sequenced each individual to ~45–71 x (Table 1), in line with the procedures used in previous studies (Keightley et al., 2015; Kong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: A total of 5.3 (Atlantic) and 5.2 (Baltic) million raw SNPs were detected in each pedigree, respectively.
source: A total of 5.3 (Atlantic) and 5.2 (Baltic) million raw SNPs were detected in each pedigree, respectively, using GATK (see Materials and methods) (McKenna et al., 2010).
evidence: This is data from the variant calling analysis.

claim: A total of 17 candidate de novo mutations were identified after stringent filtering.
source: This stringent filtering procedure identified a total of 17 candidate de novo mutations, nine in the Atlantic pedigree and eight in the Baltic one (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Nine candidate de novo mutations were identified in the Atlantic pedigree.
source: This stringent filtering procedure identified a total of 17 candidate de novo mutations, nine in the Atlantic pedigree and eight in the Baltic one (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Eight candidate de novo mutations were identified in the Baltic pedigree.
source: This stringent filtering procedure identified a total of 17 candidate de novo mutations, nine in the Atlantic pedigree and eight in the Baltic one (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Two of the 17 de novo mutations were each found in two different offspring from the same pedigree.
source: Two of the 17 de novo mutations were each found in two different offspring from the same pedigree.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2.

claim: All 17 putative de novo mutation events were confirmed to be genuine by Sanger sequencing.
source: We performed Sanger sequencing of the genomic regions around each of these putative de novo mutations in all parents and the 12 offspring (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This confirmed that all 17 putative de novo mutation events were genuine and all the peak ratios of two alleles were close to 1:1 consistent with germ-line mutations.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All the peak ratios of two alleles were close to 1:1 consistent with germ-line mutations.
source: This confirmed that all 17 putative de novo mutation events were genuine and all the peak ratios of two alleles were close to 1:1 consistent with germ-line mutations.
evidence: This is based on Sanger sequencing data.

claim: No false positives were observed in this study.
source: Thus, we did not observe any false positives in this study.
evidence: This is based on the validation of all candidate mutations by Sanger sequencing.

claim: For eight out of seventeen de novo mutations, more than one sibling carried exactly the same mutation.
source: For eight out of seventeen de novo mutations we observed more than one sibling carrying exactly the same mutation (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 2.

claim: The range of occurrences for the de novo mutations was one to nine among the 50 offspring.
source: The range of occurrences for the de novo mutations was one to nine among the 50 offspring.
evidence: This is based on transmission frequency data.

claim: The maximum observed transfer rate (18% for scaffold 153: 2,684,380 T>G) was significantly lower than the 50% expected for a fixed mutation (p=1.4×10−3, Fisher's exact test).
source: Even the maximum of the observed transfer rates (18% for scaffold 153: 2,684,380 T>G) was significantly lower than the 50% expected for a fixed mutation (p=1.4×10−3, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of transmission frequency data.

claim: About half of the de novo mutations were present in two or more offspring, indicating that they occurred during early germ cell divisions.
source: About half of the de novo mutations were present in two or more offspring, indicating that they occurred during early germ cell divisions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transmission frequency data.

claim: It would be highly unlikely to observe such a high rate of parental mosaicism unless a large fraction of the de novo mutations occurred during early germ cell divisions, assuming that the number of cell divisions from zygote to mature sperm or egg is similar in Atlantic herring to the one in mammalian species.
source: Assuming that the number of cell divisions from zygote to mature sperm or egg is similar in Atlantic herring to the one in mammalian species, we can conclude from a recent simulation study (Harland et al., 2016) that it would be highly unlikely to observe such a high rate of parental mosaicism unless a large fraction of the de novo mutations occurred during early germ cell divisions.
evidence: This is an inference based on citation to a simulation study by Harland et al., 2016.

claim: The incidence of parental mosaicism differed significantly between the two families included in this study (p=0.01, Fisher's exact test).
source: Further, the incidence of parental mosaicism differed significantly between the two families included in this study (Table 2; p=0.01, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data in Table 2.

claim: The finding that the same mutation was observed in two or more siblings for eight of the putative de novo mutations confirms that these must be germ-line mutations and not somatic mutations.
source: The finding that the same mutation was observed in two or more siblings for eight of the putative de novo mutations confirms that these must be germ-line mutations and not somatic mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transmission data.

claim: For 14 of the de novo mutations, the parental origin could be directly inferred using an additional segregating site within the same Illumina sequencing read or mate-pair read.
source: For 14 of the de novo mutations, we could detect an additional segregating site within the same Illumina sequencing read (length 125 bp) or mate-pair read that spanned the respective de novo mutation and was uniquely associated with either parent. In these cases, the parental origin could be directly inferred.
evidence: This describes the method used to determine parental origin.

claim: The parental origin of one additional de novo mutation was inferred by PCR cloning and sequencing.
source: We were able to infer the parental origins of one additional de novo mutation by PCR cloning and sequencing.
evidence: This describes the method used to determine parental origin.

claim: Out of the 15 mutations for which their parental origin was determined, there was no significant difference between paternal (eight) and maternal (seven) mutations.
source: Out of the 15 mutations for which their parental origin was determined, there was no significant difference between paternal (eight) and maternal (seven) mutations (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on data in Table 2.

claim: A paternal bias in the origin of de novo mutations has been shown in mammals, such as human (ratio = 3.9) and chimpanzee (ratio = 5.5).
source: A paternal bias in the origin of de novo mutations has been shown in mammals, such as human (ratio = 3.9) (Kong et al., 2012) and chimpanzee (ratio = 5.5) (Venn et al., 2014), where the main reason is thought to be the larger number of cell divisions during spermatogenesis than during oogenesis (Crow, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kong et al., 2012 and Venn et al., 2014.

claim: The main reason for paternal bias in mammals is thought to be the larger number of cell divisions during spermatogenesis than during oogenesis.
source: A paternal bias in the origin of de novo mutations has been shown in mammals, such as human (ratio = 3.9) (Kong et al., 2012) and chimpanzee (ratio = 5.5) (Venn et al., 2014), where the main reason is thought to be the larger number of cell divisions during spermatogenesis than during oogenesis (Crow, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crow, 2000.

claim: A binomial test against the human ratio indicates that the gender bias in herring, if it exists at all, is significantly weaker than in humans (p=0.004).
source: While the numbers are small, a binomial test against the human ratio indicates that the gender bias in herring, if it exists at all, is significantly weaker than in humans (p=0.004).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing herring and human data.

claim: In herring, both sexes produce large numbers of gametes.
source: In herring, both sexes produce large numbers of gametes and males only produce sperm during the spawning season (a few months per year).
evidence: This is established knowledge about herring reproduction.

claim: Male herring only produce sperm during the spawning season (a few months per year).
source: In herring, both sexes produce large numbers of gametes and males only produce sperm during the spawning season (a few months per year).
evidence: This is established knowledge about herring reproduction.

claim: Among the 17 de novo mutations, there were 10 transitions and seven transversions, yielding a transition/transversion ratio of 1.4.
source: Among the 17 de novo mutations, there were 10 transitions and seven transversions, yielding a transition/transversion ratio of 1.4, which can be compared with a genome-wide ratio of 1.1 for previously reported SNPs (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the detected mutations.

claim: The genome-wide transition/transversion ratio for previously reported SNPs in Atlantic herring is 1.1.
source: Among the 17 de novo mutations, there were 10 transitions and seven transversions, yielding a transition/transversion ratio of 1.4, which can be compared with a genome-wide ratio of 1.1 for previously reported SNPs (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: Kong et al. identified 3344 transitions out of 4933 events (ratio = 2.1) in humans.
source: For example, Kong et al. identified 3344 transitions out of 4933 events (ratio = 2.1) in humans (Kong et al., 2012), while Keightley et al. found five out of nine events (ratio = 1.25) in the tropical butterfly Heliconius melpomene (Keightley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kong et al., 2012.

claim: Keightley et al. found five out of nine events (ratio = 1.25) in the tropical butterfly Heliconius melpomene.
source: For example, Kong et al. identified 3344 transitions out of 4933 events (ratio = 2.1) in humans (Kong et al., 2012), while Keightley et al. found five out of nine events (ratio = 1.25) in the tropical butterfly Heliconius melpomene (Keightley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keightley et al., 2015.

claim: In humans and other mammals there is a well-established excess of CpG>TpG mutations.
source: In humans and other mammals there is a well-established excess of CpG>TpG mutations (Kong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kong et al., 2012.

claim: CpG methylations also occur in teleosts.
source: CpG methylations also occur in teleosts (Rai et al., 2010), but in our dataset only 1 out of 17 de novo mutations was of this type.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rai et al., 2010.

claim: In the herring dataset, only 1 out of 17 de novo mutations was a CpG>TpG mutation.
source: CpG methylations also occur in teleosts (Rai et al., 2010), but in our dataset only 1 out of 17 de novo mutations was of this type.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the detected mutations.

claim: The frequency of CpG>TpG mutations in herring (6%) is below, but not significantly different from the frequency reported for human (19%) (binomial test, p=0.06).
source: This frequency (6%) is below, but not significantly different from the frequency reported for human (19%) (Kong et al., 2012) (binomial test, p=0.06).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison with human data from Kong et al., 2012.

claim: There were six mutations located in intergenic regions, nine intronic mutations, one 3' UTR mutation and one exonic mutation.
source: There were six mutations located in intergenic regions, nine intronic mutations, one 3' UTR mutation and one exonic mutation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the detected mutations.

claim: The distribution of mutations across genomic regions does not deviate significantly from random expectation, given the composition of the genome after mappability filtering (p=0.65, Fisher's exact test).
source: In all, this is a distribution that does not deviate significantly from random expectation, given the composition of the genome after mappability filtering (p=0.65, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis.

claim: The estimate of the de novo mutation rate is 0.79 (19/24).
source: Since we had 12 progeny in total and two of the mutations were detected twice among the sequenced progeny, our estimate of the de novo mutation rate is 0.79 (19/24).
evidence: This is based on the number of detected mutations and the number of progeny.

claim: After strict filtering, ~442 Mb of sequence was available for variant screening.
source: After strict filtering of genomic regions with low mappability and repetitive sequences, we had ~442 Mb of sequence available for variant screening.
evidence: This describes the callable genome size after filtering.

claim: 2.6% of the 442 Mb region has insufficient depth for successful SNP calling.
source: Based on the distribution of read coverage in a random subset of the genome, we estimated that 2.6% of this region have insufficient depth for successful SNP calling, giving us a final callable region of 442 × 0.974 = 431 Mb (representing ~51% of the genome).
evidence: This is based on analysis of read coverage distribution.

claim: The final callable region is 431 Mb, representing ~51% of the genome.
source: Based on the distribution of read coverage in a random subset of the genome, we estimated that 2.6% of this region have insufficient depth for successful SNP calling, giving us a final callable region of 442 × 0.974 = 431 Mb (representing ~51% of the genome).
evidence: This is based on calculation from the filtered genome size and coverage analysis.

claim: The mutation rate per site per generation can be estimated as 1.8×10−9 (95% CI = 1.1–2.7 × 10−9, assuming that the mutations are Poisson distributed).
source: The mutation rate per site per generation can thus be estimated as 19/ (2 × 12×431 x 106)=1.8×10−9 (95% CI = 1.1–2.7 × 10−9, assuming that the mutations are Poisson distributed).
evidence: This is based on calculation from the number of mutations and callable genome size.

claim: After correcting for the estimated false negative rate (5.9%), the mutation rate is 2.0 × 10−9 (95% CI = 1.1–2.9 × 10−9).
source: If we correct for the estimated false negative rate (5.9%) we obtain: 2.0 × 10−9 (95% CI = 1.1–2.9 × 10−9).
evidence: This is based on correction for false negative rate.

claim: The minimum generation time of Atlantic herring before the onset of large-scale commercial fishing was estimated to be approximately six years based on historical sampling of several herring stocks.
source: Based on historical sampling of several herring stocks, we estimated the minimum generation time of Atlantic herring before the onset of large-scale commercial fishing to be approximately six years (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of historical data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Using the historical generation time, the mutation rate per site per year in the Atlantic herring was estimated at 3.3 × 10−10 (95% CI = 1.9×10−10 – 4.8 × 10−10).
source: Using this historical generation time, the mutation rate per site per year in the Atlantic herring was estimated at 3.3 × 10−10 (95% CI = 1.9×10−10 – 4.8 × 10−10).
evidence: This is based on calculation using the estimated generation time.

claim: The finding of a high degree of parental mosaicism for the detected de novo mutations is consistent with several recent studies indicating that the early cleavage cell divisions in the germ-line are particularly mutation-prone.
source: Our finding of a high degree of parental mosaicism for the detected de novo mutations is consistent with several recent studies indicating that the early cleavage cell divisions in the germ-line are particularly mutation-prone (Harland et al., 2016; Rahbari et al., 2016; Ségurel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harland et al., 2016; Rahbari et al., 2016; Ségurel et al., 2014.

claim: A high rate of de novo mutations at early germ-cell divisions has also been reported for Drosophila.
source: A high rate of de novo mutations at early germ-cell divisions has also been reported for Drosophila (Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2014.

claim: The estimated mutation rate (μ = 2.0×10−9) for the Atlantic herring is the lowest for a vertebrate species to date.
source: The estimated mutation rate (μ = 2.0×10−9) for the Atlantic herring is the lowest for a vertebrate species to date (Table 3); about six-fold lower than in humans.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data in Table 3.

claim: The mutation rate reflects the rate in the callable fraction of the genome, which by definition does not contain repeat regions.
source: It should be noted that this number reflects the rate in the callable fraction of the genome, which by definition does not contain repeat regions.
evidence: This is a clarification about what the mutation rate represents.

claim: Replication of repetitive regions tends to be more error-prone.
source: Thus, the true genomic average could be somewhat higher, as replication of repetitive regions tends to be more error-prone, but the decreased calling power in those regions makes diversity hard to estimate in an unbiased fashion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mutation rates in repetitive regions.

claim: The nucleotide diversities in the excluded and included parts of the genome were almost identical (π = 0.00318 and π = 0.00304, respectively).
source: This analysis showed that the nucleotide diversities in the excluded and included parts were almost identical (π = 0.00318 and π = 0.00304, respectively).
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published population data.

claim: This analysis does not indicate a major difference in mutation rates between the excluded and included parts of the genome.
source: In conclusion, this analysis does not indicate a major difference in mutation rates between the two parts of the genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity in nucleotide diversity.

claim: By combining the estimated mutation rate with the neutral diversity level (π = 0.0032) and the expected relationship π = 4 Ne μ, the estimated Ne is 4 × 105.
source: By combining the now estimated mutation rate with the neutral diversity level (π = 0.0032) found by Martinez Barrio et al. (2016) and the expected relationship between nucleotide diversity, the mutation rate and effective population size (Ne) for selectively neutral alleles (π = 4 Ne μ), we obtain an estimated Ne of 4 × 105.
evidence: This is based on calculation using population genetics theory and empirical data.

claim: The estimated Ne of 4 × 105 is larger than for most terrestrial animal species, but still much lower than the census population size of the herring, about 1012.
source: While this number is larger than for most terrestrial animal species, it is still much lower than the census population size of the herring, about 1012 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the calculated Ne and known census size.

claim: Martinez Barrio et al. (2016) showed that the herring population is expanding from a previous bottleneck using coalescent analysis and allele frequency distributions.
source: Using coalescent analysis and allele frequency distributions, Martinez Barrio et al. (2016) showed that the herring population is expanding from a previous bottleneck.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: Population genetics theory implies that it will take 4Ne generations before populations reach their genetic equilibrium.
source: Population genetics theory implies that it will take 4Ne generations before populations reach their genetic equilibrium (Kimura and Ohta, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kimura and Ohta, 1973.

claim: The generation interval in Atlantic herring is approximately six years.
source: We have estimated the generation interval to approximately six years in this study (Supplementary file 3) and a conservative estimate of the current (not long-term) Ne is 107, which appears reasonable since we estimated long-term Ne at 4 × 105 and we have evidence for population expansion (e.g. excess of rare alleles (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016)).
evidence: This is based on analysis presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: A conservative estimate of the current (not long-term) Ne is 107.
source: We have estimated the generation interval to approximately six years in this study (Supplementary file 3) and a conservative estimate of the current (not long-term) Ne is 107, which appears reasonable since we estimated long-term Ne at 4 × 105 and we have evidence for population expansion (e.g. excess of rare alleles (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016)).
evidence: This is an inference based on the long-term Ne estimate and evidence for population expansion.

claim: It will take about 240 million years before the herring populations reach genetic equilibrium.
source: These figures indicate that it will take about 240 million years before the herring populations reach genetic equilibrium.
evidence: This is based on calculation using the generation interval and current Ne estimate.

claim: It is obvious that a species with a large population size like the herring and a relatively long generation interval will never reach genetic equilibrium.
source: Thus, it is obvious that a species with a large population size like the herring and a relatively long generation interval will never reach genetic equilibrium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time required to reach equilibrium.

claim: Background selection (the elimination of deleterious alleles) and selective sweeps will lead to reductions in nucleotide diversity at linked neutral sites.
source: Background selection (the elimination of deleterious alleles) and selective sweeps will also lead to reductions in nucleotide diversity at linked neutral sites (Gillespie, 2000, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gillespie, 2000, 2001.

claim: Highly efficient purifying selection decreases the fraction of the genome that appears as selectively neutral.
source: Furthermore, highly efficient purifying selection decreases the fraction of the genome that appears as selectively neutral (Ohta, 1973) which is also expected to lead to a slightly reduced nucleotide diversity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ohta, 1973.

claim: The drift-barrier hypothesis predicts that the purging of slightly deleterious mutations affecting the mutation rate is particularly effective in species that have a very large effective population size, large fecundity and close to random mating.
source: The fact that the observed mutation rate is unusually low in the Atlantic herring is of interest in relation to the drift-barrier hypothesis (Lynch et al., 2016), which predicts that the purging of slightly deleterious mutations affecting the mutation rate is particularly effective in species that have a very large effective population size, large fecundity and close to random mating, conditions which the Atlantic herring meets (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lynch et al., 2016.

claim: The Atlantic herring meets the conditions of very large effective population size, large fecundity and close to random mating.
source: The fact that the observed mutation rate is unusually low in the Atlantic herring is of interest in relation to the drift-barrier hypothesis (Lynch et al., 2016), which predicts that the purging of slightly deleterious mutations affecting the mutation rate is particularly effective in species that have a very large effective population size, large fecundity and close to random mating, conditions which the Atlantic herring meets (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on known characteristics of Atlantic herring.

claim: The population size of the Atlantic herring appears to have fluctuated over time.
source: However, since the population size of the Atlantic herring appears to have fluctuated over time (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016), it remains unclear exactly how powerful selection has been in a time-averaged perspective, which means the support for the drift-barrier hypothesis is not unconditional.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martinez Barrio et al., 2016.

claim: The low body temperature of a marine fish may slow down the metabolic rate which has been suggested to decrease the mutation rate.
source: Additionally, the low body temperature of a marine fish may also slow down the metabolic rate which has been suggested to decrease the mutation rate (Martin and Palumbi, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin and Palumbi, 1993.

claim: Malinsky et al. (2017) used three trios representing three species of Lake Malawi cichlids and estimated the overall mutation rate to 3.5 × 10−9.
source: In a recently released study, Malinsky et al. (2017) used three trios representing three species of Lake Malawi cichlids and estimated the overall mutation rate to 3.5 × 10−9 compared with 2.0 × 10−9 for the Atlantic herring.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malinsky et al., 2017.

claim: Lake Malawi cichlids have a lower estimated effective population size than herring.
source: However, these fish both have a lower estimated effective population size than herring (Malinsky et al., 2017) and live in warmer waters.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malinsky et al., 2017.

claim: Lake Malawi cichlids live in warmer waters than Atlantic herring.
source: However, these fish both have a lower estimated effective population size than herring (Malinsky et al., 2017) and live in warmer waters.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between marine and lake environments.

claim: According to simple, ideal-case population genetic models there should be a positive relationship between nucleotide diversity and population size, so that a population at mutation-drift balance has a nucleotide diversity of 4Nμ.
source: According to simple, ideal-case population genetic models there should be a positive relationship between nucleotide diversity and population size, so that a population at mutation-drift balance has a nucleotide diversity of 4Nμ.
evidence: This is established knowledge from population genetics theory.

claim: In practice, population sizes are only weakly, if at all, correlated with nucleotide diversity.
source: In practice, population sizes are only weakly, if at all, correlated with nucleotide diversity (Leffler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leffler et al., 2012.

claim: Differences in intrinsic mutation rate is an important factor when comparing nucleotide diversities among species.
source: Our finding that the inherent mutation rate is approximately six times lower in Atlantic herring than in humans indicates that differences in intrinsic mutation rate is also an important factor when comparing nucleotide diversities among species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of mutation rates between herring and humans.

claim: In the case of the Atlantic herring, the low mutation rate, the demographic history and efficient positive and negative selection, all contribute to explaining the apparent disparity between nucleotide diversity and the census population size.
source: In the case of the Atlantic herring, the low mutation rate, the demographic history and efficient positive and negative selection, all contribute to explaining the apparent disparity between nucleotide diversity and the census population size in the Atlantic herring.
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple findings from the study.

claim: Two full-sib families were generated by crossing wild-caught Atlantic herring from Bergen (Norway) and Baltic herring from Hästskär (Sweden).
source: Two full-sib families were generated by crossing wild-caught Atlantic herring from Bergen (Norway) and Baltic herring from Hästskär (Sweden).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: For each family, six offspring from a total of 50 progeny were selected for sequencing together with the two parents.
source: For each family, six offspring from a total of 50 progeny were selected for sequencing together with the two parents.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A sample size of 12 progeny was expected to result in about 100 detectable novel mutations based on previously known vertebrate mutation rates and the size of the genomic regions that could be used to detect mutations.
source: Our aim was to determine the mutation rate to its order of magnitude and one to two significant digits. Thus, a samples size of 12 progeny was expected to result in about 100 detectable novel mutations based on previously known vertebrate mutation rates and the size of the genomic regions we could use to detect mutations.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the sample size.

claim: The sequences were aligned to the recently published Atlantic herring genome.
source: The sequences were aligned to the recently published Atlantic herring genome (Martinez Barrio et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics method used.

claim: The sequence data have been deposited in the SRA archive (PRJNA356817).
source: The sequence data have been deposited in the SRA archive (PRJNA356817).
evidence: This provides information about data availability.

claim: The false negative rate estimated using the empirical method was 5.9%.
source: The average detection rate of such heterozygous positions across all offspring was 94.1%, yielding a false negative rate of 5.9%.
evidence: This is based on analysis of heterozygous sites where parents were homozygous for different alleles.

claim: The false negative rate estimated using the simulation procedure was approximately 2.7%, while roughly 9% of sites failed to generate a call.
source: Across all offspring, we found an overall frequency of 2.7% false negative calls, while roughly 9% of sites failed to generate a call (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on simulation analysis.

claim: The two methods used to estimate false negative rate are in agreement.
source: Overall, the two methods used are in agreement.
evidence: This is a comparison of the empirical and simulation methods.

claim: Using the simulated false negative value would result in the final mutation rate being approximately 5% higher.
source: The choice has minor effects on the estimated mutation rate, as using the simulated value would result in the final rate being approximately 5% higher.
evidence: This is based on calculation comparing the two false negative rate estimates.

claim: The generation length of populations with overlapping generations is equal to the mean age of parents.
source: The generation length of populations with overlapping generations is equal to the mean age of parents (Hill, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hill, 1979.

claim: In Atlantic herring, weights and fecundity are strongly and nearly linearly correlated.
source: In our analyses we used age-specific weights as proxy for age-specific fecundity, since in Atlantic herring weights and fecundity are strongly and nearly linearly correlated (Arula et al., 2012; Oskarsson and Taggart, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arula et al., 2012; Oskarsson and Taggart, 2006.

claim: The generation time was estimated for herring stocks with data starting shortly after the end of World War II, a period characterized by still low commercial exploitation which started to increase after the early 1960s.
source: We estimated the generation time for the herring stocks with data starting shortly after the end of the World War II, a period characterized by still low commercial exploitation which started to increase after the early 1960s.
evidence: This describes the time period used for generation time estimation.

claim: The generation time was very similar for almost all the stocks in the first available period after World War II (1947-1965), characterized by low exploitation.
source: The generation time was very similar for almost all the stocks in the first available period after the World War II, characterized by low exploitation, i.e. in 1947-1965.
evidence: This is based on analysis of historical stock data.

claim: During 1947-1965, the generation time declined between ~6 years in late 1940s (corresponding to the lowest exploitation) and ~5 years in 1965, decreasing further in successive years.
source: During this period, the generation time declined between ~6 years in late 1940s (corresponding to the lowest exploitation) and ~5 years in 1965, decreasing further in successive years.
evidence: This is based on analysis of historical stock data.

claim: No data were available for the period before 1947 when the generation time was likely to have been higher.
source: No data were available for the period before 1947 when the generation time was likely to have been higher.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trend observed in the available data.

claim: The Norwegian spring spawning herring showed a higher generation time than the other stocks, oscillating around 10 years in the 1950s.
source: The Norwegian spring spawning herring showed a higher generation time than the other stocks, oscillating around 10 years in the 1950s.
evidence: This is based on analysis of historical stock data.

claim: The generation time of 6 years is considered a minimum estimate for Atlantic herring under no or moderate exploitation.
source: We therefore consider the generation time of 6 years as a minimum estimate for Atlantic herring under no or moderate exploitation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the historical data analysis.
